# Cellulose ionic conductors for sustainable ion transport in next‑generation electrochemical devices

Julian Ignacio Lopez1, Hegang Zhi1, Songtao Yang1,2, Jiushi Ma1,2, Jing Tang1,a)

Cellulose-derived ionic conductors (CICs) are emerging as sustainable alternatives to conventional ionconducting materials in electrochemical devices. This review highlights recent progress in the synthesis, functionalization, and application of CICs, focusing on cellulose nanofibers (CNF), cellulose nanocrystals (CNC), and bacterial nanocellulose (BNC). Nanocellulose materials offer unique advantages, including high surface area, tunable morphology, mechanical robustness, and environmental compatibility, making them ideal candidates for sensing and energy storage platforms. Ion transport mechanisms in solid and quasi-solid systems are discussed concerning electrostatic interactions, hydration effects, and polymer dynamics. Representative CIC examples are presented in sensors, fuel cells, supercapacitors, and solid-state batteries to showcase performance and versatility. Key challenges, including ionic conductivity limitations, scalability, and testing standardization, are briefly outlined to provide context for future research directions. Overall, this review establishes CICs as a promising material class for nextgeneration sustainable electrochemical technologies.

## Introduction

The growing demand for sustainable and high-performance energy technologies has intensified the search for eco-friendly materials capable of efficient ion transport and environmental sustainability. This trend is especially evident in sectors such as electric vehicles, long-duration grid storage, portable electronics, and commercial applications, where rapid technological advancement is accompanied by increasing pressure to replace petroleum-dependent ionic conductors (ICs) with greener, renewable alternatives [1]. ICs play a critical role in the performance of these energy devices across these applications, as they facilitate ion transport essential for both energy generation and storage. Several types of ICs are currently employed across industries, with aqueous, solid, and quasi-solid systems representing the primary categories. Recent research has increasingly focused on solid and quasi-solid conductors, as shown in the increasing number of citations per year, due to their compatibility with sustainable materials, flexibility, mechanical properties, and their potential to enable high energy density in electrochemical devices [2–4]. In addition to these inherent advantages, solid and quasi-solid materials offer several key benefits over their aqueous counterparts: (1) elimination of sealing issues associated with liquid difficulties, (2) reduced self-discharge under open circuit conditions, (3) enhanced chemical stability, and (4) greater potential for device miniaturization with thin films [5]. Specifically, among emerging biopolymer materials such as chitosan, collagen, spider silk, silkworm silk, and gelatin, cellulose has garnered increased attention due to its unique convergence of abundance, biodegradability, and functionality [6, 7]. As fields transition toward greener alternatives to synthetic polymers and toxic electrolytes, cellulose is a promising platform for renewable, high-performing ionic conductors. Beyond its sustainability, cellulose is the most abundant biopolymer on Earth and has long been used in the production of pulp, paper, packaging materials, and textiles [8, 9]. Its success in these applications is largely attributed to its distinctive molecular structure, which offers a combination of mechanical robustness, modifiable surface chemistry, fibrous architecture, and structural tunability features that are increasingly relevant for ion-conducting applications [10, 84]. Consequently, cellulose-derived ionic conductors (CICs) hold significant promise for integration into a wide range of energy-related applications, including solid-state batteries, fuel cells, supercapacitors, sensors, and bioelectronics [11–14]. Being sourced from both plants and bacteria, cellulose serves as an ideal material for bridging sustainability with the functional demands of modern energy devices, as illustrated in Fig. 1. While several reviews have addressed biopolymer electrolytes and cellulose-based materials, very few have offered a focused and up-to-date analysis of CICs specifically through

the lens of sustainable ion transport and application-oriented. This review aims to address that knowledge gap by highlighting recent progress in utilizing cellulose in various structural forms as functional components in CICs, with particular emphasis on their integration into next-generation energy device applications. This includes a detailed examination of the fundamental mechanisms of ion transport in cellulose, the strategies employed to functionalize cellulose for ionic conductivity, and an in-depth exploration of the diverse energy applications in which CICs can be implemented. Lastly, we will highlight the current technical and scientific challenges in the development of CICs and suggest future research directions aimed at overcoming these obstacles to fully realize their potential in electrochemical devices.

## Fundamentals of ion transport in cellulose

Ion transport and conduction are fundamental to the performance of the energy and sensing applications discussed in this review, including sensors, fuel cells, supercapacitors, and solidstate batteries, and represent the primary functional objective of ionic conductors. However, the efficiency of ion mobility within these materials is highly influenced by factors such as surface charge, pore size, network morphologies, and other intrinsic structural properties [15]. Accordingly, a comprehensive understanding of the structural composition of cellulose and the underlying mechanisms governing ion transport within its matrix is essential for advancing its use in these systems. These units form linear chains that are stabilized through extensive intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding, facilitated by the high density of hydroxyl groups [17, 18]. This dense hydrogen bonding network results in tightly packed molecular chains, which serve as the fundamental structural units of cellulose [17]. These chains further assemble into elementary fibrils, which collectively form the microfibrils responsible for cellulose’s characteristic nanoscale morphologies. The nanoscale morphology of cellulose varies depending on the processing technique and is commonly categorized into three main forms: (1) cellulose nanofibers or nanofibrils (CNFs), (2) cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs), and (3) bacterial (nano)cellulose (BC/BNC). Each form demonstrated superior properties to its microscale counterparts, including higher specific area, enhanced mechanical strength, and improved functional tunability [19]. Building on the established structural characteristics of cellulose, the following discussion focuses on ion transport mechanisms and the governing physicochemical principles. Ion transport within the nanochannels of cellulose-based materials is governed by three types of intermolecular interactions: hydration-related interactions (1–2 nm), van der Waals forces (1–50 nm), and electrostatic interactions (1–100 nm) involving ions at the channel’s surfaces [15, 16] Among these, electrostatic interactions are the most influential in dictating ion transport behavior, as the attraction and repulsion between mobile ions and fixed charges on the cellulose backbone strongly govern ion dissociation, mobility, and selectivity. Hydration interactions are the next most significant, particularly in quasisolid materials, where the presence of bound water or polar solvents facilitates solvation, reduces ion-ion association, and enhances ionic conductivity. In contrast, van der Waals forces do not directly mediate ion transport but play a supporting role by influencing polymer chain packing, network integrity, and fibril interactions, thereby indirectly affecting ion diffusion pathways within the material matrix [15, 16]. Beyond these primary intermolecular interactions, ion transport within CICs can be broadly classified into two categories based on the presence or absence of solvent: solvent-free systems (solid CICs) and solvent-containing systems (quasi-solid CICs). ## Methods in functionalizing nanocellulose

A multi-step process is typically required to functionalize cellulose for use as an ionic conductor [27–30]. Initially, the selected form of nanocellulose, whether CNF, CNC, or BNC, must first be extracted from the microscale fibers within the plant or microbial cell walls. Following this, surface modification is performed to introduce functional groups tailored to the intended ionic conduction application. In some cases, the functionalized nanocellulose may undergo an additional step involving composite formation or doping to further enhance conductivity or mechanical stability [27]. The modified materials are then subjected to filtration and cast into a desired

shape or structure using specific techniques [31]. Finally, the material is integrated into devices for application. This overall workflow will be examined in detail to provide a comprehensive understanding of the strategies used to functionalize cellulose for ionic conductivity. In the preparation of nanocellulose, CNFs are typically produced through a combination of chemical pretreatments and intensive mechanical fibrillation, while CNCs are commonly obtained via acid hydrolysis or oxidative methods [32]. In contrast, BNC is produced through various forms of cultivation and offers a simpler and often more cost-effective synthesis route, as it is a highly pure form of cellulose that naturally lacks lignin, hemicellulose, and other plant components [33]. Given this reason, this section will place greater emphasis on the synthesis and processing of CNFs and CNCs. Methods for extracting cellulose nanofibers

CNFs are composed of aggregated nanofibrils with typical diameters ranging from 5 to 50 nm and lengths extending up to several micrometers. Prior to nanofibrillation, raw cellulose usually undergoes a biomass purification process involving pulping and bleaching [31, 34]. The pulping step primarily removes unwanted bulk components such as lignin and hemicellulose and is commonly carried out using alkaline agents, organic solvents, or sulfur-containing compounds in combination with alkaline. Following pulping, the partially purified cellulose is subjected to a bleaching process, typically employing agents such as hydrogen peroxide or sodium chlorite. This step removes residual lignin, whitens the pulp, and enhances the overall purity of the cellulose [31]. Following the biomass purification process, cellulose undergoes further refinement through a combination of chemical treatments and mechanical disintegration. While mechanical fibrillation plays a dominant role in the production of CNFs, some attention is directed toward chemical pretreatment methods, most notably, TEMPO-mediated oxidation, originally developed by Akira Isogai and colleagues [35, 36]. This oxidative process employs a combination of reagents, such as 2,2,6,6-tetramethylpiperidine-1-oxyl (TEMPO), sodium hypochlorite, sodium bromide, and hydrochloric acid, to selectively oxidize the C6 primary hydroxyl groups on the glucose units of cellulose into carboxylate groups under alkaline conditions (pH 10–11). This modification enhances fiber hydrophilicity, reduces inter-fibril bonding strength, and promotes individual fiber segregation, thereby facilitating more efficient nanofibrillation. After the chemical pretreatment, various mechanical fibrillation techniques can be used to produce CNFs. Among the most widely utilized methods are microfluidization, fine grinding, ball grinding, and high-intensity sonification. In the microfluidization process, pretreated CNFs are first distributed in water to form a suspension, which is then pumped through a high-pressure intensifier pump [31]. The resulting suspension is forced through narrow microchannels, generating high-velocity colliding streams, intense shear forces, turbulence, and cavitation. These mechanical effects facilitate the disruption of hydrogen bonding between cellulose chains, thereby reducing fiber size to the nanoscale [37]. In fine grinding, the cellulose suspension is passed between rotating and stationary disks, where it is subjected to compressive and shear forces. In comparison, ball grinding involves mixing the cellulose suspension and milling material (ceramic, zirconia, or metal balls) inside a rotating container, where mechanical collisions cause fibrillation. Although both grinding methods are effective in producing CNFs, their high mechanical input can potentially compromise fiber integrity, leading to reduced crystallinity, mechanical strength, and

thermal stability [38]. High-intensity sonification is the other widely utilized method wherein ultrasound waves are applied to a cellulose suspension, inducing cavitation, the formation, expansion, and implosion of microscopic gas bubbles. These generate localized shear forces capable of breaking down cellulose aggregates into CNFs [39]. Sonification is particularly valued for its cost-effectiveness, energy efficiency, and environmental friendliness, making it a compelling option for sustainable CNF production [31].

Methods for extracting cellulose nanocrystals

CNCs are rod-like nanoparticles typically characterized by diameters ranging from 2 to 20 nm and lengths exceeding 100 nm. Similar to CNFs, the production of CNCs begins with a biomass purification step to remove non-cellulosic components. The detailed process for the purification of CNF/CNC is described in Sect. “Methods for extracting cellulose nanofibers.” CNCs are primarily synthesized through acid hydrolysis, oxidative treatments, and solvent-based extraction methods [40–43]. Acid hydrolysis is the most employed method, wherein the amorphous regions of cellulose are selectively degraded, while the crystalline domains remain intake due to their resistance to acid penetration [44]. This process involves treating purified cellulose with controlled concentrations of acid at a specific temperature to cut glycosidic bonds within the amorphous regions, associated with hemicellulose, thereby isolating the crystalline segments as elongated particles [31, 45]. Mild acid concentrations (1–10 wt%) are typically utilized for pretreatments, while more concentrated solutions (30–70 wt%) are employed to achieve higher crystallinity and faster reaction rates. Common acids used for hydrolysis include sulfuric acid, hydrochloric acid, and metal salt catalysts [46, 47]. Additionally, organic acids such as maleic or formic acid have been explored as more environmentally sustainable alternatives, offering the potential for reagent recovery and recycling. Among the oxidative methods for synthesizing CNCs, TEMPO-mediated oxidation is the most widely employed. Similar to its application in CNF productions, TEMPO-oxidized cellulose fibers are subjected to extended ultrasonication or other mechanical agitation to facilitate the isolation of nanocrystals. The TEMPO-oxidation process for CNCs, which is similar to that of CNF, is described in detail in Sect. “Methods for extracting cellulose nanofibers.” Among solvent-based extraction methods for CNCs, two approaches have gained widespread use, the first being ionic liquids (ILs). IL-assisted extraction involves the disruption of hydroxyl groups on the cellulose surface, which are responsible for intra- and intermolecular hydrogen bonding [45, 48]. Methods for extracting bacterial nanocrystals

BNC is a highly pure, nanoscale form of cellulose synthesized via microbial fermentation, primarily by aerobic bacteria such as Komagataeibacter, Acetobacter, and Escherichia. During the fermentation process, nutrients are partially utilized for bacterial growth, while the remainder is converted into cellulose, carbon dioxide, water, and energy [58]. Optimal BNC production is achieved under controlled conditions of pH, temperature, oxygen availability, and substrate concentration and can be carried out using static, agitated/shaking, or bioreactor-based cultivation methods [59]. Static cultivation, which involves incubating nutrient solutions in stationary containers, typically yields dense hydrogel films with high strength, compact texture, and favorable water permeability. However, this method is limited by slow production rates and low overall yield. In contrast, agitated or shaking cultures involve continuous movement of the fermentation containers, which enhances oxygen and nutrient diffusion [59]. This approach supports increased microbial activity and enables the formation of BNC in various morphologies, including pellets, spheres, and fibrous structures [60]. Nevertheless, BNC produced under agitated conditions generally exhibits lower crystallinity, mechanical strength, and degree of polymerization compared to static cultivation. Bioreactor cultivation offers a scalable alternative and typically employs either stirred tank or airlift designs. These systems enhance oxygen transfer

and biomass circulation, promoting faster growth and higher productivity [58]. However, they are associated with higher equipment costs and challenges such as BNC adhesion to reactor surfaces [61]. Despite differences in cultivation methods, the fundamental biosynthetic pathway of BNC remains consistent. It involves four primary steps: activation of monosaccharides, polymerization of glucose units, optional simultaneous addition of acyl groups, and extrusion of cellulose through the wall/ membrane complex [60].

## Applications and performance evaluation

As mentioned in the introduction, cellulose-derived ionic conductors (CICs) take advantage of their abundant hydroxyl groups and highly modifiable nanostructures to form functional materials with high mechanical strength, biodegradability, flexibility, and high specific surface area. Owing to its advantageous properties and highly modifiable structure, CICs have been applied across a range of emerging technologies, including sensors, fuel cells, supercapacitors, and solid-state batteries. The following subsections examine these application areas and present representative examples of recent CIC developments along with their corresponding performance characteristics.

Sensors

Sensors are functional devices that detect and respond to physical, chemical, or biological stimuli by converting them into measurable electrical or optical signals. This signal transduction capability enables their integration into diverse application areas, including wearable devices, biomedical devices, and soft robotics. Typically, sensors fulfill three core functions: detecting changes in a target stimulus, transducing the sensed input into a quantifiable signal, and transmitting the signal to a processor for interpretation or action. To perform reliably under dynamic and often mechanically demanding conditions, the ionic conductors used in such sensors must possess a combination of properties, including high ionic conductivity, mechanical robustness, flexibility, and biocompatibility, many of which align closely with the inherent characteristics of CICs. Through the sol–gel transition method of poly (vinyl alcohol) and CNFs in a dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO)-water solvent, Ye et al. successfully synthesized hydrogels with outstanding properties for use in multifunctional sensors [65]. The presence of interconnected crystalline and amorphous domains within the polyvinyl alcohol (PVA)-CNF hydrogel contributes to its exceptional mechanical performance, including high stretchability (660%), high strength (2.1 MPa), and high toughness (5.25 MJ ­m−3), attributed to the reinforcing effect of CNF, as demonstrated in Fig. 4(a and b). Fuel cells

Fuel cells represent a promising green energy technology that generates electricity through an innovative electrochemical process. Their operational principle relies on proton exchange membranes (PEMs) that facilitate directional proton transport while supporting electron flow through an external circuit. Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs), in particular, rely heavily on membrane performance to achieve high energy conversion efficiency. While Nafion membranes have been widely used due to their high proton conductivity (0.1–0.2 S ­cm−1 under hydrated conditions) and durability, their reliance on water-mediated transport significantly limits performance at elevated temperatures (> 80 °C), where dehydration reduces conductivity and necessitates complex external humidification systems [68]. These limitations have spurred interest in alternative PEM materials with enhanced thermal and operational stability. Among emerging candidates, cellulose-derived membranes offer significant promise due to their low production cost, environmentally benign synthesis methods, structural tunability, and potential to be functionalized, making them a compelling platform for PEM development and other components within fuel cells. PEMs synthesized predominantly from cellulose present a clear economic advantage over commercial alternatives like Nafion. While their power density currently remains lower than that of Nafion-based systems, their significantly reduced production cost makes them attractive for further development. Bayer et al. employed spray deposition techniques to coat sulfonated CNFs directly onto the catalyst layer of a fuel cell, effectively decreasing membrane resistance and enhancing ionic conductivity, which leads to improved power density [69]. The resulting cellulose-derived PEMFC achieved a current density of 0.8 A ­cm−2 and a power density of 156 mW ­cm−2.

Notably, the estimated production cost of the cellulose membrane was approximately 50 USD ­m−2, significantly lower than Nafion’s 750 USD ­m−2, underscoring the potential of cellulosederived PEMs for large-scale manufacturing and cost-effective fuel cell technologies [69]. Beyond cost advantages, cellulosederived PEMs also offer environmental benefits compared to conventional methods. The synthesis of traditional PEMs often involves fluorination and sulfonation, processes that generate non-degradable byproducts with long-term environmental consequences. In contrast, recent efforts have focused on developing green synthetic routes and designing sustainable PEMs from cellulose and its derivatives. For instance, Huang et al. fabricated a membrane using CNCs grafted with cytidine monophosphate (CMP), taurine (TAU), and cysteine (Cys), achieving improved proton conductivity while preserving biodegradability and avoiding fluorinated reagents [69], as demonstrated in Fig. 5(a). The resulting membrane exhibited a methanol permeability of 2.46 × ­10–7 ­cm2 ­s−1 and a power density of 34.05 mW ­cm−2, approaching that of Nafion. Similarly, Yang et al. modified BNC with 3-aminopropyltriethylsilane (APTES) to prepare a fully bio-based PEM incorporating alkaline proton conductors [70]. This membrane demonstrated enhanced proton conductivity (62.2 mS ­cm−1) and thermal stability, reaching a power density of 4.85 mW ­cm−2, surpassing that of unmodified bacterial cellulose membranes. In addition to their role as proton exchange membrane applications, cellulose-derived materials can also be tailored to function as anion exchange membrane materials for fuel cell applications. Ni et al. developed a nanoporous hydroxide ion conductor based on BC, incorporating a layered double hydroxide (LDH) structure to enhance ion transport [71]. The channellike architecture formed by the LDH-nanocellulose composite facilitated efficient hydroxide ion conduction, yielding a conductivity of 4.254 × ­10–2 S ­cm−1 [Fig. 5(b and c)]. The membrane also demonstrated excellent mechanical integrity, contributing to a peak power density of 84.2 mW ­cm−2, approximately twice that of comparable chitosan/BNC-derived fuel cells. Apart from their utility in membranes, nanocellulose is increasingly being explored as a component for low-cost electrodes in fuel cells. Mashkour et al. investigated a microbial fuel cell (MFC) designed for cost-effective, low-rate power generation [72], as shown in Fig. 5(d). The researchers developed a membrane electrode using BC in combination with carbon nanotubes and nano-zycosil. In this configuration, the BC served not only as a mechanically robust scaffold but also played a key role in promoting ionic and electronic conductivity by supporting uniform dispersion and interconnection of conductive additives. The resulting composite electrode achieved a power density of 920 mW ­m−2, exhibited enhanced voltammetric capacitance, and demonstrated a significantly lower internal resistance of 0.8kΩ compared to conventional gas diffusion electrodes [Fig. 5(e and

Supercapacitors

Supercapacitors are advanced energy storage devices characterized by excellent cycling stability, structural simplicity, and tunable design parameters, garnering significant research interest. Their distinct electrochemical design enables high power densities and faster charge–discharge rates compared to conventional metal-ion batteries, though with relatively lower energy storage capacity. As such, supercapacitors are often deployed as rapid-response energy storage components in high-power demand systems [74]. Their structural adaptability enables integration into diverse application sectors, including flexible

and wearable electronics as well as thin-film energy devices. Operating through ion polarization, electrostatic adsorption at the electrode–electrolyte interface, and high-rate faradaic redox reactions, to store and release electrical energy. Through the supercapacitor context, CICs have gained attention for their favorable ionic conductivity, mechanical robustness, and environmental sustainability. As integrated solid-state electrolytes in supercapacitors, CICs offer superior structural versatility and tunability compared to conventional solid-state electrolytes. Kasprzak et al. demonstrated that gel polymer electrolytes based on cellulose and chitosan, incorporating the ionic liquid 1-ethyl-3-methylimidazolium tetrafluoroborate ­(EMImBF4), achieved a wide electrochemical window (up to 3.0 V) and excellent cycling stability, retaining 90% capacity after 10,000 cycles [Fig. 6(a)] [75]. This performance is attributed to the enhanced ionic conductivity enabled by replacing the aqueous phase in the hydrogel with ionic liquid, while the gel matrix maintains effective ion transport pathways. In applications like wearable electronics, where mechanical flexibility and biocompatibility are prioritized over maximum conductivity, cellulose-derived electrolytes offer clear advantages. A recent study by Xu et al. highlighted the limitations of conventional hydrogel electrolytes, including poor mechanical resilience and limited thermal tolerance, which restrict their utility in variable environmental conditions, as illustrated in Fig. 6(b and c) [76]. Solid‑state batteries

In metal-ion batteries, polymer-based ion conductors, such as those derived from cellulose, are increasingly employed to fabricate solid-state electrolytes due to their advantageous properties. Unlike conventional liquid electrolytes, solid-state ion conductors offer improved safety, potential for higher ionic conductivity, and greater energy storage capacity. However, traditional inorganic solid-state ion electrolytes often suffer from intrinsic brittleness and rigidity, leading to poor interfacial contact and reduced overall efficiency. While polymer-based solid-state electrolytes offer enhanced flexibility and interface compatibility, their ion transport is typically limited by ion hopping and the segmental motion of polymer chains, resulting in suboptimal ionic conductivity (as described in Sect. “Fundamentals of Ion Transport in Cellulose”) and compromising energy density. To overcome these limitations, extensive efforts are underway to develop advanced ion-conducting architectures, with cellulosederived materials emerging as a promising platform to their inherent modifiability, structural tunability, and capacity to form continuous ion transport networks. ## Challenges and future directions

This review has demonstrated that CICs are capable of addressing key needs in next-generation electrochemical systems, including sensors, fuel cells, supercapacitors, and solid-state batteries, due to their many favorable benefits. As detailed in this review, their numerous advantages make them strong candidates for replacing conventional synthetic ion-conducting materials. However, widespread implementation remains limited by several critical challenges. These include relatively low ionic conductivity, difficulties in large-scale processing, limited long-term operational stability, and the lack of standardized performance metrics across different application domains. Particularly, the reliance on ion hopping and segmental motion for ion transport, the scalability of functionalization techniques, and inconsistent characterization protocols hinder progress in the field. Addressing these limitations will require coordinated, interdisciplinary research efforts that draw upon materials science, electrochemistry, and chemical engineering. Nonetheless, recent advances show promise. Strategies such as tailoring nanocellulose morphology (pore size and structure), incorporating ion-exchange groups, and integrating redox-active sites have improved conductivity. Additionally, the optimization of pretreatment and extraction methods has made nanocellulose more accessible for functionalization. Beyond material-level design, the development of hybrid systems, such as cellulose-carbon composites, cellulose-polymer blends with reactive groups, and clay-based hybrids, has helped mitigate issues related to mechanical and thermal stability for long-term operation. Looking forward, several key directions may be prioritized. First, establishing standardized testing protocols for properties (ionic conductivity, pressure, frequency) and mechanical performance (strain rate, dimension control) is essential for cross-comparison and validation across studies. Advanced characterization tools can support this by enabling multimodal validation of transport and structure. Techniques such as small- and wide-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS/WAXS), ssNMR, thermogravimetric analysis, and operando methods can contribute to a more rigorous understanding of structure–property relationships in CICs to help establish those standardized protocols [88–90]. Second, enhancing the robust performance of CICs under extreme conditions (high/low temperature, pressure, or mechanical cycling) will expand their applicability to more demanding environments. This is especially important for accelerating broader adoption, as future materials must outperform existing systems across diverse real-world conditions, broadening their application

## Conclusion

Cellulose-derived ionic conductors (CICs) represent a rapidly advancing class of sustainable materials with tremendous potential across a range of electrochemical applications, including sensors, fuel cells, supercapacitors, and solidstate batteries. Their appeal lies not only in their renewable and biodegradable nature but also in their structural tunability, functionalizable surface chemistry, and favorable mechanical and electrochemical properties. Specifically, cellulose nanofibers (CNFs), cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs), and bacterial (nano)cellulose (BC/BNCs) have emerged as particularly promising due to their high surface area, intrinsic porosity, and compatibility with environmentally benign processing routes. This review has presented a comprehensive overview of the current state of CICs, detailing the physicochemical mechanisms governing ion transport, the primary methods of synthesis and functionalization, and their integration into a wide array of electrochemical systems. Particularly, the inclusion of representative examples of CICs successfully employed in energy and sensing devices has been highlighted to demonstrate the multifunctionality and performance benchmarks across various platforms. While the field has made substantial strides, challenges remain in scalability, long-term operational stability, and the standardization of performance metrics. Continued advancements in materials design, system development, and device engineering will be critical to overcome these barriers. As global demand for sustainable, high-performance technologies intensifies, CICs are well-positioned to contribute meaningfully to the transition toward greener energy storage and sensing platforms. Their integration into practical devices

offers not only technical advantages but also an opportunity to accelerate the adoption of circular and eco-conscious material systems.
